source.title: When Attribution Patching Lies: Diagnosis and a Second-Order Correction

page_placements.theme: Attribution approximations depend on component and model

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates IOI head rankings against activation-patching ground truth and compares attribution and correction methods, bearing on the circuit’s measured recovery and method dependence, but it is not a replication of the original circuit-identification procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports IOI head-ranking errors and recovery results, a GPT-2 IOI head case study, corruption-condition results, and GPT-2 IOI circuit-level benchmark metrics. It does not report a knockout of everything outside the proposed 26-head circuit or patching tests establishing the roles of all seven classes.
record.test_reason: The study uses GPT-2 IOI as a benchmark for attribution-patching accuracy. Its ground truth is the activation-patching head ranking under name-swap corruption, not the Wang et al. circuit. Its top-K overlap, top-5 error and MIB metrics compare its own HVP/MS-HVP correction with AP, IG, IH, GIM and EAP-IG. It never checks whether the 26-head circuit, its classes, backup heads or prompt variants hold. Method agreement is measured against activation patching, not against the original circuit, so V4 is not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that attribution-patching error comes mainly from downstream network curvature, not local nonlinearity. They propose a reliability score and HVP/MS-HVP correction that reduce error and improve recovery of the activation-patching head ranking. They state that HVP does not by itself address circuit completeness or minimality.
record.recipe_differences: The original study identifies and tests a proposed IOI circuit using causal interventions and faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria. This paper evaluates attribution-based head rankings against activation-patching effects and compares HVP corrections and other localization methods; it does not repeat the original circuit-validation protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: IOI top-5 relative error and head recovery vary by attribution/correction method. GPT-2 IOI AP median relative error also differs by corruption condition (zero versus resample). The paper reports different outcomes across MIB metrics (CPR, CMD, and average faithfulness).

fits_no_version.finding: Under name-swap corruption, first-order attribution patching underestimates the duplicate-token head L4H11 by 4.4×. It ranks 27th versus 7th by activation patching.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-based attribution patching can miss IOI circuit heads that activation patching ranks highly.

record.problems: The paper does not test the original circuit as a whole by removing components outside it, and does not establish all proposed head-class roles or completeness/minimality. The GPT-2 IOI ranking results are based on 50 prompts; the main Table 2 reports N=100, while circuit-ranking metrics are described as point estimates. MIB metrics do not directly establish the original claim’s criteria.
record.rows_left_out: No additional GPT-2 IOI head-ranking or circuit-level results relevant to these versions were omitted. Results on other models and other tasks were not included where they did not test the same GPT-2 IOI head classes and roles.

untested.parts: All: the 26 heads, the 7 classes, faithfulness, completeness and minimality.
All. Other models are run only to benchmark estimators.
All. Methods are compared with activation patching, not with the original circuit.
All. Corruption choice varies estimator error, not circuit faithfulness.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'ground truth' is activation patching, not the Wang et al. circuit. Its counts of circuit heads are inconsistent: the 'canonical boundary' has 20 heads, Figure 10 outlines 23 'known IOI circuit heads', and Figure 11 plots 18. It does not compare its top-K sets with the 26-head circuit. The prompt count is also inconsistent: the text says 50 IOI prompts, while Table 2 lists N=100. The study is best treated as a methods paper that uses IOI as a benchmark.

versions.untested_parts: Tests IOI head-ranking recovery against activation-patching effects, but does not establish the 26-head count, all seven class roles, the original faithfulness/completeness/minimality criteria, or whether removing everything outside the circuit changes IOI performance.
No ablation of main name-mover heads followed by a test of takeover by backup heads.

Although IOI localization results include other models, the paper does not establish that the same head classes and roles carry IOI across models, checkpoints, or sizes, or that components are reused for other tasks.
Compares attribution and correction methods on IOI recovery, but does not compare a broad set of circuit-finding methods, ablation types, and metrics under a common original-circuit evaluation.

Tests differences across attribution methods, reported metrics, and corruption conditions; does not vary circuit knockout types or IOI prompt distributions/templates to test those sources of sensitivity, nor directly quantify what fraction of total IOI behavior the circuit explains.
No systematic comparison across name orders, templates, or numbers of names, and no test of whether those variants use different components or heuristics.

relation.reason: The duplicate-token role is inherited from prior work. Estimator accuracy and recovered rankings do not test whether the catalog's circuit claims hold.

tranche.reason: Uses IOI to benchmark attribution estimators against activation-patching rankings and reports its own method's performance; it does not independently validate the claimed circuit or head roles.

source_check.notes: Both rows accurately record method comparisons, but should remain outside claim-testing evidence. The authors explicitly state that HVP alone does not address circuit completeness or minimality.
